COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Brown — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color brown: teddy-bear brown, pretzel brown, the color of warm and cozy.

What is this?

Brown is a color — the color of the bear, the pretzel, the mushroom and the coffee cup on the card. It is the color nearly every mixing pot makes by accident: brown is what happens when colors get friendly.

What does it mean?

Brown is the earth color: soil, tree trunks, teddy fur, baked bread. It is the most common color in nature and the coziest one in the crayon box.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "brown", find brown in toys and snacks, and hear the big idea — mix ALL the colors and brown usually arrives.

Why this matters

Brown has a marketing problem among kids and the card fixes it: brown is not boring, brown is BEARS. The coziest card in the deck gets the coziest lesson.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, a first theory idea (all colors mixed = brown), texture words (fuzzy bear, twisty pretzel), and snack anchoring — the tastiest color card by a mile.

Words to learn

brownbearpretzelmushroomcoffee cupteddycozyhugtwistwarm

Say this to your child

“"Brown! The bear is brown, the pretzel is brown, the mushroom is brown, the coffee cup is brown. Brown is the cozy color — teddy color, warm bread color. Where is YOUR brown teddy?"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: bear — brown, pretzel — brown, mushroom — brown, coffee cup — brown. Three snacks and one bear; the bear is technically also a snack, for hugs.
  2. Teddy audit: fetch every brown teddy in the house to the rug. Name each one brown as it arrives. The pile IS the lesson.
  3. The big mix idea: what do you get when you mix ALL the colors? Usually brown — the mud color, the tree-trunk color, the color the whole forest stands on.
  4. Pretzel geometry: pretzels are twisty — trace the twist on the card with one finger, then twist arms and bodies into pretzel shapes. A knot is fine. Knots are the point.
  5. Close with the coffee cup: whose cup at home looks like that one? (Somebody’s always does.) Grown-ups raise the real one — the card’s toast.

Look closer at the picture

The bear square is the only one with a face — the pretzel, mushroom and cup are all things grown-ups make. Brown is the color of things we bake, and one thing we hug.

Ask your child

"Which brown thing gives the best hugs?" (bear — obviously) "Which brown thing is twisty?" (pretzel) "What grows brown in the forest, with a cap?" (mushroom)

What your child can say or do

Your child might line up every brown toy for a "brown parade" or demand a pretzel with scientific urgency. Both outcomes are the lesson succeeding.

Out in the real world

Pretzels are baked brown in ovens everywhere; real mushrooms grow in forests and — the safety note — only grown-ups pick them. The teddy bear is named after a president, Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt, which is the square’s grown-up fact.

Try it together

Teddy picnic: blanket down, brown toys invited, real or pretend pretzels served, and every arrival announced — "the brown bear is here!" Sorting, naming, hosting. Clean-up is the bear parade home.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the bear?" (brown) "What do you get if you mix ALL the colors?" (usually brown!) "Find something brown in this room." (the teddy audit says it worked)

This lesson pairs with the Brown flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.
